questions.q: Why does the lesson call 'walk me through a project' the single highest-leverage interview question to prepare for?
options: It's almost universal, and it's the one question where preparation, not just knowledge, fully determines how well you answer
Because it is the only question ever asked in quantum computing interviews
Because it only applies to candidates with a PhD
Because it requires no prior preparation at all
questions.explain: The lesson explains this question's near-universality and that preparation (structuring your capstone narrative in advance) is what separates a strong answer from a weak one, more than raw knowledge alone.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why does including the confound/unexpected-result story in a 'walk me through a project' answer tend to make candidates seem MORE credible, not less?
options: Because interviewers always prefer longer answers regardless of content
Because confounds are required content by interview policy
Interviewers who have done real research themselves respond well to candidates who can describe handling an unexpected result honestly, more than candidates describing only clean successes
Because clean successes are considered suspicious and are never believed
questions.explain: The lesson states that a candidate who only reports a clean success on a first real research-style project often reads as LESS credible to an interviewer who has done real research -- the honest confound-and-correction story is a stronger signal.

questions.q: What does the lesson recommend doing when asked a technical question you genuinely don't know the answer to?
options: Guess confidently and hope the interviewer doesn't check the answer
End the interview immediately
Say so plainly, then reason toward a partial answer from what you do know, rather than guessing confidently
Change the subject to a different topic you're more comfortable with
questions.explain: The lesson frames honest acknowledgment followed by reasoning from related knowledge as the strong move, consistent with the course's overall honesty principle -- not confident guessing.

questions.q: Which of these is listed as a recurring quantum computing interview category?
options: Questions exclusively about unrelated classical web development frameworks
Hardware/noise reasoning -- explaining why a circuit behaves differently on real hardware than in simulation, and what mitigation could help
Questions that never involve any live coding or whiteboard work
Questions only about company history and founding date
questions.explain: The lesson lists fundamentals checks, algorithm walk-throughs, hands-on coding, hardware/noise reasoning, and project walk-throughs as the recurring categories -- hardware/noise reasoning draws directly on Chapters 1-2's content.

questions.q: What does the lesson's closing note say this entire 14-course path has, and has NOT, honestly prepared a student to do?
options: It guarantees a job at a quantum-native hardware company immediately upon completion
It has prepared nothing of real value, per the lesson's own admission
It has fully prepared students for any research-scientist role at any national lab with no further study

It has prepared real, hireable software/algorithmic work at the Developer/Algorithms Engineer tier; it has NOT manufactured a shortcut into research-scientist or hardware-lab roles, which still require graduate study
questions.explain: The lesson's closing note draws this exact honest distinction, consistent with Lesson 25 and Lesson 27's framing throughout the chapter -- real preparation for one tier, explicit honesty about what remains out of reach without graduate study.
